blocks.x: Pronunciation in Japanese has two elements: the sounds themselves (vowel/contant) and the intonations on each mora (a mora is basically a syllable). The former is relatively easy to learn, though there are some things that may give you difficulty like the “fu” sound, the “ra” row (ra,ri,ru,re,ro) and the “o” vowel. However, once you learn to hear the sounds and get your tongue and mouth to make the right shapes, I think you can probably pronounce reasonable sounds.

But the intonations (high, low) are a different story, and are one of the hardest parts of the language to master. There are a few reasons. First, it is not just “high” and “low” pitches, but in longer runs of “high” pitches the pitch actually continues to raise a little. Second, pitches differ between regional dialects, so unless you are careful you might accidentally pick up a non-Tokyo dialect (which is fine, as long as that is how you want to talk). Also, intonation patterns differ between words in a fairly irregular way, not to mention that one word can sometimes affect the next word’s pitch!

Fortunately, there are a handful of rules that help you here. One of my favorite rules about intonation patterns is how all i-adjectives follow the “accented” pattern (more formally 起伏式, [kifukushiki], which means the accent starts low and rises until it reaches the mora before the “i” (the second to last) and then drops suddenly.
Even though the pitches are not simply high and low, we can still use notation to get an idea of what the pitches look like. For example, let’s look at “aoi” (blue):
青い => L/H/L [aOi]
Here, the pitch goes up for the “o” part in “aoi”, then drops on the “i”. Another:
安い [yasui] => L/H/L [yaSUi].
Note that this is not an emphasis accent like English, but rather the pitch rises and falls.

A long time ago I read somewhere that all i-adjectives followed this pattern, and purposefully tried to emulate that in my speech. However, when doing some research recently for my new educational site Japanese Vocab Maker, I made a shocking discovery: that there are actually a few exceptions to this rule!

It turns out some of the common i-adjectives are actually flat or monotone (平板式 [heibanshiki]). The good news is that there is a relatively small number of everyday words with this pattern. Here is a list of such words:
赤い [akai] = red (L/H/H) [aKAI]
甘い [amai] = sweet (L/H/H) [aMAI]
重い [omoi] = heavy (etc)
軽い [karui] = light
黄色い [kiiroi]: yellow
茶色い [chairoi]: brown
遠い [tooi]: far
粗い [arai]: rough
重たい [omotai]: heavy
To hear the difference, tou can listen to a native pronounce “aoi” vs “akai” in these two linked videos.
Furthermore, it turns out that a bunch of i-adjectives can be pronounced in either monotone or accented. Here is a partial list of those:

明るい, 厚い, 危ない, 薄い, おいしい, 遅い, 固い, 暗い, 冷たい, 辛い, 丸い, 難しい, 優しい, 眠い, 悲しい, 易しい, 浅い, 怪しい, きつい, 四角い, 分厚い, 危うい, 堅い, 気まずい, たやすい, 手厚い, 程遠い, よろしい, だるい, 細長い, 乏しい, 望ましい, 目新しい, 疑わしい, 煩わしい, むなしい, 重苦しい, 堅苦しい, 気恥ずかしい, 口やかましい, 荒っぽい, 恐れ多い, 多い, たわいない.

I wouldn’t memorize the above list, though. I think the best strategy is just to memorize the earlier list of monotone-only words (akai, amai, etc.), and then use accented for the rest. At leat until you hear a native speaker do otherwise.
